module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Pierce–Birkhoff conjecture

*Reference:* [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierce%E2%80%93Birkhoff_conjecture)

The Pierce-Birkhoff conjecture asserts that any piecewise-polynomial function can be expressed
as a maximum of finite minima of finite collections of polynomials. It was first stated in 1956
by Garrett Birkhoff and Richard S. Pierce, though the modern rigorous formulation is due to
Melvin Henriksen and John R. Isbell.

The conjecture has been proved for `n = 1` and `n = 2` by Louis Mahé.
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace PierceBirkhoff

/--
A set is semi-algebraic in `ℝⁿ` if it can be described by a finite union of sets, each defined by
finitely many simultaneous multivariate polynomial equations and strict inequalities.
-/
def IsSemiAlgebraic {n : ℕ} (S : Set (Fin n → ℝ)) : Prop :=
  ∃ (ι : Type) (p₀ p₁ : ι → Finset (MvPolynomial (Fin n) ℝ)), Finite ι ∧
    S = ⋃ i, {x | (∀ p ∈ p₀ i, MvPolynomial.eval x p = 0) ∧
      ∀ p ∈ p₁ i, MvPolynomial.eval x p > 0}

/--
A set is semi-algebraic in `ℝ` if it can be described by a finite boolean combination
of polynomial equations and inequalities.
-/
def IsSemiAlgebraic₁ (S : Set ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∃ (ι₀ ι₁ : Type) (p₀ : ι₀ → Polynomial ℝ) (p₁ : ι₁ → Polynomial ℝ), Finite ι₀ ∧ Finite ι₁ ∧
    S = (⋃ i, {x | Polynomial.eval x (p₀ i) = 0}) ∪ ⋃ i, {x | Polynomial.eval x (p₁ i) > 0}

open scoped Polynomial

/--
A function `f : ℝⁿ → ℝ` is piecewise polynomial if there exists a finite covering of `ℝⁿ` by
closed semi-algebraic sets such that the restriction of `f` to each set in the covering is
polynomial.
-/
def IsPiecewiseMvPolynomial {n : ℕ} (f : (Fin n → ℝ) → ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∃ (ι : Type) (P : ι → Set (Fin n → ℝ))
    (g : ι → MvPolynomial (Fin n) ℝ),
    Finite ι ∧
    (∀ i, IsClosed (P i)) ∧
    (∀ i, IsSemiAlgebraic (P i)) ∧
    (⋃ i, P i) = Set.univ ∧
    ∀ᵉ (i : ι) (x ∈ P i), f x = MvPolynomial.eval x (g i)

/--
A function `f : ℝ → ℝ` is piecewise polynomial if there exists a finite covering of `ℝ` by
closed semi-algebraic sets such that the restriction of `f` to each set in the covering is
polynomial.
-/
def IsPiecewisePolynomial (f : ℝ → ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∃ (ι : Type) (P : ι → Set ℝ)
    (g : ι → Polynomial ℝ),
    Finite ι ∧
    (∀ (i : ι), IsClosed (P i)) ∧
    (∀ (i : ι), IsSemiAlgebraic₁ (P i)) ∧
    (⋃ (i : ι), P i) = Set.univ ∧
    ∀ᵉ (i : ι) (x ∈ P i), f x = Polynomial.eval x (g i)

/--
The Pierce-Birkhoff conjecture states that for every real piecewise-polynomial function
`f : ℝⁿ → ℝ`, there exists a finite set of polynomials `gᵢⱼ ∈ ℝ[x₁, ..., xₙ]` such that
`f = supᵢ infⱼ(gᵢⱼ)`.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 13]
theorem pierce_birkhoff_conjecture {n : ℕ} (f : (Fin n → ℝ) → ℝ)
    (hf : IsPiecewiseMvPolynomial f) :
    ∃ (ι κ : Type) (g : ι → κ → MvPolynomial (Fin n) ℝ), Finite ι ∧ Finite κ ∧
      ∀ x, f x = ⨆ i, ⨅ j, MvPolynomial.eval x (g i j) := by
  sorry

/--
The Pierce-Birkhoff conjecture holds for `n = 1`.
This was proved by Louis Mahé.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 13]
theorem pierce_birkhoff_conjecture_dim_one (f : ℝ → ℝ)
    (hf : IsPiecewisePolynomial f) :
    ∃ (ι κ : Type) (g : ι → κ → Polynomial ℝ), Finite ι ∧ Finite κ ∧
      ∀ x, f x = ⨆ i, ⨅ j, Polynomial.eval x (g i j) := by
  sorry

/--
The Pierce-Birkhoff conjecture holds for `n = 2`.
This was proved by Louis Mahé.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 13]
theorem pierce_birkhoff_conjecture_dim_two
    (f : (Fin 2 → ℝ) → ℝ) (hf : IsPiecewiseMvPolynomial f) :
    ∃ (ι κ : Type) (g : ι → κ → MvPolynomial (Fin 2) ℝ), Finite ι ∧ Finite κ ∧
      ∀ x, f x = ⨆ i, ⨅ j, MvPolynomial.eval x (g i j) := by
  sorry

end PierceBirkhoff

reformulations.difference: The definition uses only finite unions of individual polynomial zero sets and strict positivity sets, rather than explicitly allowing arbitrary finite Boolean combinations.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: This is equivalent in one real dimension. The finitely many roots of the nonzero polynomials occurring in a Boolean description partition ℝ into finitely many points and open intervals on which every polynomial has constant sign. Thus every semialgebraic set is a finite union of selected points and intervals. A point {a} is defined by x-a=0; a bounded open interval (a,b) by (x-a)(b-x)>0; and open rays by x-a>0 or a-x>0. Included endpoints are added as points. Empty and universal sets are also expressible. Conversely, the finite unions in the Lean definition are themselves Boolean combinations of polynomial conditions. Scratch proofs verify these building blocks and closure under union, but not the complete classification equivalence.

reformulations.difference: The existential finite index types for the supremum and infimum need not be nonempty, whereas finite maximum/minimum expressions ordinarily use nonempty families.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For nonempty finite types, Lean's real indexed suprema and infima equal finite maxima and minima. If either index type is empty, this expression is identically zero: real empty suprema and infima are zero, and the supremum of a constant-zero family is zero. That adds no representable functions because the zero function already has a representation using two singleton index types and the zero polynomial. The converse is immediate. The scratch file proves the representation predicate equivalent to the version requiring both types to be nonempty, and verifies the finite max/min identities.

reformulations.difference: The finite supremum/infimum index types may be empty.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Empty indices produce only the identically zero function, already representable with singleton indices and the zero univariate polynomial. Nonempty finite indexed extrema are genuine maxima/minima. The scratch file proves the equivalence with a representation requiring nonempty index types, including its specialization to Polynomial ℝ.

reformulations.difference: The finite supremum/infimum index types may be empty.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: As in the general-dimensional statement, empty indices produce only zero, which has a singleton-index zero-polynomial representation. The scratch equivalence is proved for MvPolynomial (Fin n) ℝ for arbitrary n, hence applies to n=2. Nonempty finite extrema equal maxima/minima.

review.notes: Checked all four definitions and all three theorems. The piecewise-polynomial definitions match Definition 1.1 of the primary reference; their finite closed covers imply continuity, as also proved in the scratch file. The representation witnesses are quantified before the evaluation point, so one global finite polynomial family is required. A common inner index type is harmless: differing finite row lengths can be padded by repeating polynomials. The n=0 case is valid because its domain has one point and every function on it is constant. General/open and dimension-one/two/solved statuses agree with the cited sources. /workspace/review/scratch.lean compiles successfully and contains auxiliary equivalence proofs, empty/universal-set checks, interval and singleton constructions, polynomial and absolute-value examples, and the n=0 representation. The checked proofs do not depend on sorryAx. The reviewed file remains identical to its committed blob.
